extracted.intended_audience: researchers/experimenters in psychophysics, anthropometry, and human-measurement (19th-century scientific audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and conducting hands-on experiments and records to measure human (and animal) sensory discrimination and bodily measurements, and summarising those measurements statistically. Includes apparatus design, test protocols, recording practices, and statistical summarisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a geometric series of test weights
rubrics_metrics.description: The weights are proportioned so that their register numbers (1,2,3,...) are the logarithms of their weights, hence the weights run in a geometric series and the numbers form a scale of equal degrees of sensitivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a person can just distinguish weights differing by 2 register steps (e.g. 1 and 3) he will similarly distinguish any pair differing by 2; someone distinguishing adjacent numbers has twice the delicacy. This principle underlies objective testing across senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protocol: pairwise then triplet testing with eyes shut
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial testing by handing pairs of weights until approximate discrimination is found, then more carefully presenting shuffled sequences of three weights to be arranged in order by the operatee with eyes shut.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record the scale interval the operatee can just appreciate as the true measure of coarseness (or inverse of delicacy). Perform tests on several separate occasions; brief practice improves results but routine familiarity usually gives stable measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: General principle: stimuli graded geometrically produce arithmetic sensation increments
rubrics_metrics.description: When stimuli increase by geometric grades, the sensations they give rise to will increase by arithmetic grades, provided the stimulus is neither barely felt nor so strong as to excite fatigue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle justifies constructing test sequences in geometric progression for touch, taste, smell, hearing, etc., to create equal subjective steps of sensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for non-target sensory cues (stimulus similarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparatus/stimuli must be alike in all respects except the intended stimulus dimension (e.g. weight), because visible or tactile differences will vitiate judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use identical external forms (e.g. mechanically-made cartridge cases), handle items in a bag or with eyes shut, and guard against external stains, balance differences, uneven packing, or internal motion that provide alternative cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of multidimensional mechanical/tactile properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Two objects equal in weight and appearance may differ mechanically (e.g. internal motion, distribution of mass, oscillation period) and thus be distinguishable by touch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test for such differences (spin eggs, suspend and tap cartridges to observe oscillation) and design stimuli to avoid confounds; acknowledge that apparently simple perceptions are complex and easily influenced by unintended attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparatus design for high-frequency hearing tests (graduated whistle)
rubrics_metrics.description: A small whistle with a variable-length bore (graduated plug) to vary pitch and determine the upper audible limit of individuals; graduations allow precise note identification via a table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the whistle to rapidly find an individual's limit for shrill notes. Expect a noticeable fall-off with age; subjects may be unconscious of their deficiency and may resist the test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal hearing tests: behavioural response interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a whistle on a walking-stick to produce shrill notes near animals and observe responses (e.g. pricked ears) to infer hearing ability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure animals are accustomed to the instrument and heedless; absence of response may indicate inaudibility or lack of attention. Different species and sizes vary (cats highly sensitive; large dogs often not).

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish anthropometric registers (periodic standardised records)
rubrics_metrics.description: Create laboratories where individuals may periodically be weighed, measured, photographed (full face and profile on same scale), and have bodily faculties tested by best-known methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such routine records (growth charts, photos, measurements, notes of events) are necessary for appraising effects of external conditions on development and for later biographical and eugenic research; batch photography and autotype reproduction reduce cost and fading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family histories and multigenerational data collection
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage families to compile chronological photographic portraiture and physical records across generations, accompanied by medical and life-history notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These domestic registers will be invaluable for future investigators of human heredity and eugenics. Make the practice easy, low-cost, and habitual so opportunities are not lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement is necessary because people are unconscious of peculiarities
rubrics_metrics.description: Many individuals are unaware of sensory defects (e.g. deafness to high notes, colour blindness) and do not betray them to friends; hence objective measurement is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on self-report or casual observation; apply specific tests to reveal deficiencies (careful colour-matching, high-note whistles, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical summarisation using the ogive (smooth frequency curve)
rubrics_metrics.description: Large groups of the same species exhibit a smooth 'ogive' frequency curve when ordered (median at centre with fewer extremes); this follows from many minute independent causes of variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent distributions by plotting ordinates at convenient fractional parts (median, quartiles, octiles/deciles). Five ordinates (median, quartiles, deciles) usually suffice for practical purposes and allow reconstructing the ogive approximately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and practical use of centesimal grades (percentiles)
rubrics_metrics.description: When defining an individual's position in a series, give the centesimal grade (0–100) corresponding to their rank, noting that rank positions correspond to graduations half a place short (e.g. rank 5 of 27 corresponds to graduation 4.5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Rule of Three to convert ranks to centesimal grades; in large classes half-place differences are negligible so rank and graduation may be treated as identical for practical use. Examples provided illustrate calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of comparing two groups by corresponding centiles
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare two statistical groups by stating the centesimal grade in one group that corresponds to the median (or any other fractional grade) in the other; this is independent of theory and applicable whenever ordering is possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This simple correspondence succinctly expresses relative merits between groups and is applicable to physical or mental qualities whenever members can be sorted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field recording technique for quick pairwise comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Carry an inconspicuous pricker and a prepared cross-shaped paper to mark quick comparative judgments ('more', 'same', 'less') in the field without attracting attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange paper into three compartments (head for 'more', solitary arm for 'same', long foot for 'less'), write the subject of measurement on the paper beforehand, and accumulate multiple records in the pocket for later tabulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about subgrouping and species definition in statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: When subdividing groups to seek more specific species, exercise judgment: too much subdivision yields groups too small for statistical value; too little yields groups that are not truly specific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'species' may be defined as a group whose individual differences result from combinations of many minute causes with no single dominant cause. The smoothness of the ogive is evidence of appropriate grouping; a broken outline suggests confusion of species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider demographic and social history when interpreting prevalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Population history (e.g. endogamy, sectarian marriage rules) can change prevalence of hereditary traits (example: higher colour-blindness prevalence among Quakers due to historical isolation and emigration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for segregation, selective emigration/desertion, and marriage patterns in interpreting frequency differences between groups; such causes combine with heredity to alter trait prevalence.
